119 README.md # time-i-gram **A grammar for interactive visualization of time-based data.** time-i-gram extends [Gosling.js](https://github.com/gosling-lang/gosling.js) with a temporal field type, time-aware data sources (`csv-time`, `json-time`), a time axis, time coordinate systems (calendar periods such as "week of the year" and offsets relative to an event), calendar units with aggregation, and time transforms. A visualization is a JSON spec; `embed` renders it, with zooming, brushing and linked views. This package is a single self-contained ES module: React, PixiJS, HiGlass and their CSS are bundled, so there is nothing else to install. The grammar, the editor with examples and the source code: https://github.com/vanessastoiber/time-i-gram ## Install From a CDN, nothing to install: ```js import { embed } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/time-i-gram@0.1.0/dist/index.js'; ``` With a bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack, ...): ```bash npm install time-i-gram ``` ```js import { embed } from 'time-i-gram'; ``` ## Usage in a plain HTML page ```html
``` `embed(element, spec, options?)` returns a promise of the visualization's API (zoom to a range, subscribe to events, export images). ## Usage in Observable In an [Observable notebook](https://observablehq.com), `embed(spec)` returns an element that the cell displays: ```js embed = (await import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/time-i-gram@0.1.0/dist/index.js')).embed ``` ```js embed({ /* a time-i-gram spec */ }) ``` In [Observable Framework](https://observablehq.com/framework/): ```js import { embed } from 'npm:time-i-gram@0.1.0'; display(await embed({ /* a time-i-gram spec */ })); ``` ## TypeScript The package includes types for `embed` and for specs: ```ts import { embed, type GoslingSpec } from 'time-i-gram'; ``` ## Citation If you use time-i-gram in your research, please cite: > V. Stoiber, D. Chacón-Ramírez, N. Gehlenborg, W. Aigner, and M. Streit, "time-i-gram: A Grammar for > Interactive Visualization of Time-based Data," Center for Open Science (preprint), 2026. > doi: [10.31219/osf.io/m9ubg_v2](https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/m9ubg_v2) ```bibtex @article{Stoiber2026, title = {time-i-gram: A Grammar for Interactive Visualization of Time-based Data}, doi = {10.31219/osf.io/m9ubg_v2}, url = {https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/m9ubg_v2}, publisher = {Center for Open Science}, author = {Stoiber, Vanessa and Chacón-Ramírez, Denisse and Gehlenborg, Nils and Aigner, Wolfgang and Streit, Marc}, year = {2026}, month = aug } ``` ## License MIT. time-i-gram is built on [Gosling.js](https://github.com/gosling-lang/gosling.js) (MIT) and [HiGlass](https://github.com/higlass/higlass) (MIT). total 6932 drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Nov 4 08:44 . drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Nov 4 08:44 .. -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 60071 Nov 4 08:44 gosling.schema.d.ts -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 469 Nov 4 08:44 index.d.ts -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 7022842 Nov 4 08:44 index.js Shell cwd was reset to /work

content.text:
I built the calendar heatmap in `/work/spec.json`. It renders without errors, but the console logs some warnings. The years 2012–2026 run top to bottom, one per row, with ISO weeks left to right.

**What it shows:** most years peak in winter and are lowest in summer. 2020 and 2021 break that cycle: activity dropped from spring 2020 (lowest in week 23, 196 per 100,000), and early 2021 had no winter wave. I checked the peak and low weeks for each year against the raw file.

**How it works:** the file is loaded straight from the RKI URL as tab-separated. It is filtered to `Bundesweit` / `00+`, and the `Kalenderwoche` values are read as ISO weeks. The x axis is wrapped by ISO week-based year, which also creates the year field used for the rows. Week 53 appears only in 2015 and 2020, the two years in the data that have one.

**Two workarounds:**
- **Row order:** the row channel has no sort option, and by default 2012 appeared at the bottom. I listed the years 2012–2026 by hand as the row order. No data values are typed in.
- **Legend:** a legend inside the heatmap covered the cells. Following the repository's own Beijing example, I put the legend in a second track with the same data drawn invisible, so its scale still comes from the data.

**Render log:** status OK. The log has 11 console warnings: "unknown data type", "No dataConfig children" and a bare stack trace. None of them stopped the rendering. I did not track down where they come from.

```
REPORT
deliverable: spec.json
requirements:
  R1: done - one row per ISO year 2012-2026, top to bottom; order set by a hand-listed row domain
  R2: done - one cell per ISO week (week-based year period), W1 left; W53 shown for 2015 and 2020
  R3: done - viridis sequential scale; legend "per 100k/wk", full unit in legend track title
  R4: done - weeks before 2012-W40 and after 2026-W43 are blank
  R5: done - week ticks every 8 weeks (W1, W9, ...); year labels on each row
  R6: done - title plus one-sentence caption as subtitle
assumptions:
  - ISO year = week-based year of Kalenderwoche, not the Saison column
  - Row order given as an explicit list of the years 2012-2026 (grammar has no sort for row); leading '' row leaves room for the track header, as in the repo example
  - Caption is in the subtitle; data source is in the track title
limitations:
  - Year list has to be edited by hand when the data reaches 2027
  - Week axis labels every 8th week, not every week
  - Legend sits in a separate track below the heatmap, with an invisible copy of the data
  - Legend title is shortened ("per 100k/wk"); the full unit is in the legend track title
  - Render log has console warnings (unknown data type, dataConfig, bare stack trace); not traced
```
